title: Prism deviation and dispersion

sources.title: NTA: Official JEE Main 2026 syllabus, Physics Unit 16

chapters.title: Nonparallel faces change the final direction
chapters.formula: r1 + r2 = A; deviation delta = i + e - A
points: A is the prism apex angle in the principal section.
i and e are measured from the normals to their respective faces.
The transmitted two-face path must exist before applying the relations.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. A parallel slab shifts a ray sideways but returns it to a parallel direction. A prism has faces that are not parallel, so the ray generally emerges in a different direction. We describe that change by its angle of deviation. Work in the prism's principal section and draw a normal at each face. The entry angle is i. The internal angles are r one and r two, each measured from its local normal. The emergence angle is e. Geometry gives r one plus r two equal to the prism angle A. The overall deviation equals i plus e minus A for the ordinary transmitted path. Suppose A is sixty degrees, i is forty-five, and e is fifty. The deviation is thirty-five degrees. The incidence and emergence angles are not measured from the prism faces, and they do not share one common normal. That is why a quick sketch is so valuable. The relation assumes that the ray enters and leaves through the two intended faces. At some internal angles, total internal reflection can prevent that emerging path. Then blindly calculating an emergence angle gives a nonphysical answer. Our prism drawings are geometry guides, not scale-accurate trajectories for every choice of index. Start with the path, label the two normals, and only then use the angle sum.

chapters.title: Minimum deviation is the symmetric path
chapters.formula: At minimum: i = e, r1 = r2 = A/2; n_relative = sin((A+delta_min)/2)/sin(A/2)
points: Same surrounding medium on both sides, homogeneous prism.
The symmetric transmitting path gives the usual minimum deviation.
The result uses a relative refractive index, not automatically an absolute one.
chapters.script: Rotate an ordinary prism while keeping the incoming ray fixed. The deviation first decreases, reaches a minimum, then increases. At that minimum for the usual symmetric setup, the internal ray takes a symmetric path: i equals e, and r one equals r two. Since the internal angles add to A, each is A over two. Combine this with Snell's law at the entry face. The prism's index relative to its surroundings equals sine of half of A plus minimum deviation, divided by sine of half of A. Let's use a sixty-degree prism with minimum deviation thirty degrees. Half of A plus that deviation is forty-five degrees; half of A alone is thirty degrees. The ratio is sine forty-five divided by sine thirty, or square root of two. This is about one point four one four. If the surrounding medium is air approximated as index one, it is also the prism's approximate absolute index. In another surrounding medium, multiply by that medium's index to obtain the absolute prism index. Do not use the minimum-deviation formula when the given path is not at minimum. And do not assume i equals e for every orientation. The equality is the special symmetry condition we earned by choosing the minimum path, not a universal prism rule.

chapters.title: Find minimum deviation from index
points: The inverse-sine argument must not exceed one.
Angles in this numerical example are degrees.
An index can rule out the intended symmetric transmitting path.
chapters.script: Now reverse the problem. We know a prism's refractive index and want its minimum deviation. For a sixty-degree glass prism in air with index one point five, the internal angle at symmetry is thirty degrees. Snell's law gives sine i equal to one point five times sine thirty, or zero point seven five. The incidence angle is about forty-eight point six degrees. Minimum deviation is twice that angle minus sixty, approximately thirty-seven point two degrees. Let's pause for an error check. Is the index ratio below one? No, so the ray bends toward the normal on entering, consistent with an incidence angle larger than the thirty-degree internal angle. And is the sine argument physically allowed? Zero point seven five is below one. Good. In general, delta minimum equals twice the inverse sine of relative index times sine of half the prism angle, minus A. If that inverse-sine argument exceeds one, the usual symmetric transmitted path cannot exist. A calculator error is telling us something physical, not asking for a creative replacement number. Keep degree and radian modes consistent. These angle relations do not require a small-angle approximation. The thin-prism shortcut coming next does, and we should not silently swap the two formulas.

chapters.title: A thin prism gives a useful approximation
chapters.formula: For small A and small ray angles: delta approximately (n_relative - 1) A
points: Use radians when deriving sin theta approximately theta.
Use the same angular unit for A and delta after applying the ratio.
The approximation is not intended for a large-angle prism.
chapters.script: For a thin prism, with a small apex angle and sufficiently small incidence and refraction angles, Snell's law simplifies because sine theta is approximately theta in radians. At entry, i is approximately relative index times r one. At exit, e is approximately relative index times r two. Add the two equations and use r one plus r two equal to A. Subtract A, and we get deviation approximately relative index minus one, times A. So a small four-degree prism with index one point five in air gives an approximate deviation of two degrees. We derived the relation using radians, but the proportional result works with degrees too when A and deviation use the same angular unit. This shortcut is not for the sixty-degree prism from our earlier example. Applying it there would give thirty degrees instead of the more accurate thirty-seven point two at minimum. The discrepancy is a warning about the approximation, not a contradiction in optics. If a JEE question explicitly says a thin prism and gives small angles, this relation can save time. Otherwise use Snell's law and the actual prism geometry. The reason a larger index gives more deviation in this ordinary setup is that each interface bends the ray more relative to its normal.

chapters.title: Dispersion separates colors through different indices
chapters.formula: Normal dispersion: n_violet > n_red, so delta_violet > delta_red in the ordinary prism setup
points: Frequency is conserved at a stationary boundary.
A prism separates spectral components; it does not create their frequencies.
Index ordering is wavelength-dependent and not universal in every spectral region.
chapters.script: A prism can spread white light into colors because its refractive index depends on frequency. In the ordinary visible normal-dispersion region of glass, violet has a larger index than red. Violet is therefore deviated more in the usual prism arrangement. The prism is not changing red light into violet light. At stationary interfaces the frequency of each component stays the same. It redirects the components by different amounts. For a thin four-degree prism, suppose red has index one point five zero and violet has index one point five two. Red deviation is approximately two degrees. Violet deviation is two point zero eight degrees. Their angular separation is zero point zero eight degrees. Small, but quite measurable with a suitable arrangement. That example also shows why we distinguish deviation of a single color from dispersion between two colors. If both indices increased equally, both deviations could change without changing their separation by the same amount. The violet-more-than-red ordering describes ordinary normal dispersion, not every material at every frequency. Near absorption bands, behavior can differ. Finally, remember that total internal reflection and dispersion are different effects: one concerns whether a transmitted ray exists, while the other concerns how index varies across spectral components. Our JEE routine is to identify the regime, label angles, and apply the appropriate exact or approximate relation.
